why_this_tool: SGLang puts continuous batching, automatic prefix cache reuse, grammar-constrained output, an OpenAI-compatible server and a routing gateway in one engine, so every idea in this lesson can be practised with a single tool.
alternatives: vLLM (PagedAttention-based engine with the widest community adoption and a similar OpenAI-compatible server), Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (a packaged container server; as of 2026-10 it is in maintenance mode and its repository is archived, and Hugging Face points to vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and MLX instead), NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM served through NVIDIA Dynamo or Triton (a runtime tuned for NVIDIA GPUs; as of 2026-10 current releases have no separate engine-build step, since the TensorRT backend was removed in release 1.2), llama.cpp or Ollama (CPU-friendly quantized serving for a laptop, not built for high-concurrency GPU batching).

setup.do: Install SGLang into a fresh Python virtual environment using the package installer method in the installation page.
setup.done_when: Importing sglang in the virtual environment succeeds and prints a version number.
setup.why: A clean pinned environment keeps the engine's heavy dependencies away from other projects and makes the later reproduce steps honest.

setup.do: Start a model server with a small open-weight chat model from the Hugging Face Hub; full speed needs an NVIDIA GPU, so on a laptop without one pick the smallest supported model and expect slow output.
setup.done_when: The server log reports that it is ready and listening on the local port.
setup.why: Every later step talks to this running server, and choosing a tiny model keeps download time and memory within laptop limits.

setup.do: Install the SGLang Simulator from the SGLang repository as the no-GPU substitute for load experiments.
setup.done_when: The simulator server starts locally without asking for a GPU.
setup.why: The simulator lets you study scheduling and batching behaviour under load on a laptop where a real GPU run is not possible.

setup.do: Install the SGLang Model Gateway using the Python package option, after checking its prerequisites.
setup.done_when: The gateway launch command prints its help text listing routing and worker options.
setup.why: The gateway is the routing layer used in the registration and production-like steps, so it has to be available before the path reaches them.

steps.do: Run your first chat completion against the local server by following the quickstart request example.
steps.done_when: A JSON response containing generated text and a token usage block is printed in the terminal.
steps.why: A single successful round trip proves the model loaded, the tokenizer works and the HTTP server is reachable before anything else is layered on.

steps.do: Run the same request with streaming enabled and watch the tokens arrive one at a time.
steps.done_when: Output appears incrementally as separate chunks, and you can state the delay before the first chunk versus the gap between later chunks.

steps.why: This makes visible why LLM serving differs from classic model serving: generation is autoregressive, the request holds memory for its whole lifetime, and latency splits into time to first token and time per token.

steps.do: Query the server through the OpenAI Python client by pointing its base address at the local SGLang endpoint.
steps.done_when: The unmodified client library returns a chat completion from the local model.

source.title: Tutorial: Sending a request - SGLang Documentation

steps.why: An OpenAI-compatible endpoint is what lets application teams swap a hosted model for a self-hosted one without changing client code, which is the contract a platform engineer has to keep.

steps.do: Read the Model Gateway architecture section and sketch how the control plane, data plane and workers relate to the single server you have been running.
steps.done_when: You have a one-page diagram naming the worker, the router, the control plane and the data plane and what each one owns.
steps.why: Workers, routers and the split between registering capacity and routing requests are the core objects of an SGLang deployment, and the later steps assume this vocabulary.

steps.do: Configure the memory and scheduling arguments on a server restart, lowering the static memory fraction and the maximum number of running requests, then compare this design with the paged block allocation that PagedAttention introduced in vLLM.
steps.done_when: The startup log shows a different cache pool size for each setting, and you can explain in two sentences how vLLM pages the same memory.
steps.why: Both engines exist to pack many concurrent sequences into a fixed key-value cache pool, and changing these arguments shows directly how cache capacity limits concurrency.

steps.do: Run several requests that share a long identical system prompt, note the cached token counts in the server log, then call the flush cache endpoint and send the request again.
steps.done_when: The log shows cached tokens for the repeated prefix before the flush and none on the first request after it.
steps.why: Prefix reuse is the signature SGLang optimisation: a shared prefix is computed once and reused, so flushing the cache shows the cost that reuse was saving.

steps.do: Write a JSON schema for a small record and send a request constrained to it through the OpenAI-compatible API, then compare the output with an unconstrained run of the same prompt saved to a file.
steps.done_when: The constrained response parses against the schema on every run, while the saved unconstrained response fails or drifts at least once.
steps.why: Structured generation guarantees parseable output by masking tokens during decoding, and keeping both outputs side by side shows what the constraint changes.

steps.do: Load a small embedding model on a second port and request embeddings in the compact base64 response format.
steps.done_when: The response carries a base64 string instead of a float list, and its byte size is smaller than the default response for the same input.
steps.why: Platform teams serve embedding models next to chat models, and the compact encoding shrinks response payloads noticeably for high-volume retrieval traffic.

steps.do: Start the gateway in co-launch mode so that it brings up the router and its workers together and registers them behind a single address.
steps.done_when: A request sent to the gateway address is answered, and the gateway log names the worker that handled it.
steps.why: Registering workers with a router is how a model is promoted from a lone process to an addressable service that can gain or lose capacity.

steps.do: Run a concurrent benchmark workload (use the simulator when there is no GPU), then compare throughput and latency before and after adjusting the settings that raise token usage.
steps.done_when: You have a two-row table of throughput and latency for the default and tuned settings, with the token usage figure observed for each.
steps.why: Benchmarking and tuning an endpoint means driving it to a target latency and cost, and token usage in the log is the first signal of whether the server is saturated or idle.

steps.do: Enable deterministic inference on the server and run the same prompt several times at different levels of concurrent load.
steps.done_when: Repeated runs of the same prompt return byte-identical output whatever other requests are in flight.

source.title: SGLang for RL Systems - SGLang Documentation

steps.why: Batch-dependent numerical differences make regression checks flaky, so a deterministic mode is what lets an automated pipeline compare outputs across builds.

steps.do: Read how llm-d provides a Kubernetes-native gateway for SGLang and map each piece onto a local cluster such as kind or minikube; real GPU nodes are out of reach on a laptop, so treat this as a design exercise.
steps.done_when: You can list the Kubernetes resources that would sit in front of your SGLang workers and what each one decides.
steps.why: Kubernetes deployment of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint adds inference-aware routing and scaling on top of the engine, and knowing which component does what comes before writing any manifest.

steps.do: Deploy a production-like topology locally by launching two workers as separate processes and then starting the gateway separately in front of them over HTTP.
steps.done_when: Requests to the gateway are spread across both workers, and stopping one worker leaves the endpoint still answering.
steps.why: Separating router and worker lifecycles is how real fleets roll out, scale and replace capacity without dropping the public endpoint.
